facility_roles.quote: NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory, jointly funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation and the U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Science, is a brand new astronomy and astrophysics facility on Cerro Pachón in Chile.

intervals.label: concept and community recommendation
intervals.note: The history page says planning began in the early 1990s and that a 2001 report recommended the telescope as a major initiative; no formal proposal date is given, so the year of the 2001 recommendation is used as the start of the proposed interval.
intervals.quote: a 2001 report by the Astronomy and Astrophysics Survey Committee

intervals.label: construction
intervals.note: The photo caption dates the First Stone event to April 2015. End: October 2025 official transition from construction to operations.
intervals.quote: In 2015 a traditional stone-laying ceremony was held on Cerro Pachón, in Chile, to commemorate the official start of construction.

intervals.label: system commissioning
intervals.locator: Rubin 'History' page, section 'Bringing it all together'
intervals.note: Start is the month the LSST Camera was installed on the telescope; the page also describes an earlier 2024 campaign with the Commissioning Camera and does not give a single commissioning start date. The DOE announcement says the survey start followed "final commissioning work, an operational readiness review, and the beginning of the alert stream". End is the LSST start.
intervals.quote: In March 2025, the LSST Camera — the largest digital camera in the world — was installed on the telescope

Rubin Observatory is operated by NSF NOIRLab and SLAC and has no single experiment collaboration; the LSST Dark Energy Science Collaboration (the dark-energy science group of the survey, one of the Rubin LSST science collaborations) is attached as the collaboration for this dark-energy record.
Atlas kind dark_energy_survey is the closest A26 kind; Rubin is also a Solar System, Milky Way and transient survey (see physics goals).

Sources disagree on the month: the Rubin survey-strategy page says "as of June 29, 2026"; the Rubin LSST page says "in June 2026"; the Rubin About page says "in July 2026"; the DOE Office of Science announcement is dated 30 June 2026. 29 June 2026 is used (the only day-precision statement from a Rubin page).

physics_goals.quote: Understanding the nature of dark matter and dark energy Creating an inventory of the Solar System Mapping the Milky Way Exploring the changing sky
physics_goals.value: Advance four science areas: the nature of dark matter and dark energy, an inventory of the Solar System, a map of the Milky Way, and the changing sky.

summary.plain: A ten-year survey that photographs the whole southern sky every few nights with the largest digital camera ever built, on a Chilean mountaintop. Its repeated images chart dark matter and dark energy and reveal asteroids, exploding stars and a changing sky.
summary.technical: The Legacy Survey of Space and Time with the 8.4-m Simonyi Survey Telescope and the 3.2-gigapixel LSST Camera at Rubin Observatory, Cerro Pachón. Began 29 June 2026 for ten years, revisiting each field about 800 times in six bands; designed for dark energy and dark matter, the Solar System, the Milky Way and the transient sky.
